noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how the process of respiration produces ATP in living organisms
know that ATP provides energy for cells

primer.text: Respiration happens in every living cell, quietly and constantly. This note pins down what the process actually is — a chemical reaction, not the breathing that feeds it — and follows the energy it frees into ATP, the currency every cell spends on movement, growth and warmth.

lessons.title: Respiration Is a Chemical Reaction
lessons.opening: Respiration is the chemical reaction run by all living organisms that breaks down glucose — with oxygen when available, without it when not — releasing energy that is transferred into ATP.
keyPoints: Every living organism carries out respiration.
Glucose is the fuel broken down in the reaction.
Oxygen marks the aerobic version; its absence marks the anaerobic one.
Carbon dioxide and water are the usual waste products.
The released energy is transferred as ATP.

low.restatement: All cells break down glucose and bank the released energy as ATP.
low.analogy: A power plant burning fuel to send electricity down the line — the line here is ATP.
low.examPointer: Keep respiration and gas exchange separate: one moves gases, the other spends glucose.

medium.restatement: Whether oxygen joins or not decides the pathway, but both versions transfer energy, and the aerobic one also yields carbon dioxide and water.
medium.analogy: Two routes up the same mountain: one needs gear, one does not, and both get you higher.
medium.examPointer: If a question says energy is 'produced', correct it: energy is released or transferred, never made.

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Plants, fungi and microbes respire too.
Even cells lacking mitochondria run respiration.
Respiration runs day and night in every living cell.

check.stem: Which molecule is the fuel that respiration breaks down?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Oxygen supports the aerobic route; it is not the fuel.
Starch is storage; glucose is the molecule actually broken down.
ATP is the carrier produced, not the fuel consumed.

check.stem: How is respiration different from gas exchange?

options.text: Gas exchange moves gases in and out, while respiration uses them to release energy from glucose
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They are two names for one process
options.explanation: The distinction is a standard exam trap.
No ATP comes from exchange alone.

options.text: Respiration only happens in the lungs
options.explanation: Respiration happens in cells throughout the body.

check.stem: In which form does respiration hand over its released energy?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Glucose is spent, not handed over.
Heat is one use of the energy, not the transfer molecule.
ADP gains a phosphate to become ATP during the process.

check.stem: Which statement about the wastes of aerobic respiration is right?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water leave as waste products
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Oxygen is consumed, not released.
Lactic acid marks the oxygen-free animal route.
The reaction does produce wastes despite releasing energy.

check.modelAnswer: Respiration is the chemical reaction in all living organisms that breaks down glucose to release energy transferred as ATP.

check.stem: Name the two waste products of the aerobic pathway.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water are the wastes of aerobic respiration.

check.stem: Explain why energy is described as transferred rather than produced in respiration.
check.modelAnswer: Because the energy already exists in the glucose bonds; the reaction releases it from storage into ATP rather than creating anything new.

check.stem: A poster claims 'Mitochondria make energy'. Rewrite it accurately.
check.modelAnswer: Mitochondria release energy from glucose during aerobic respiration, transferring it into ATP.

lessons.title: ATP, the Spent Currency
lessons.opening: ATP molecules forged during respiration are broken down again wherever work is needed, paying for reactions that build larger molecules, for every muscle contraction and for the warmth that keeps enzymes working well.
keyPoints: Cells produce several ATP molecules as glucose is broken down.
Breaking ATP down releases energy for living processes.
Building larger molecules from smaller ones consumes ATP.
Muscle contraction draws on ATP for movement.

low.restatement: Respiration fills ATP wallets; cell work empties them.
low.analogy: Rechargeable batteries: charged by respiration, drained by every job the cell does.
low.examPointer: List the three classic uses: building molecules, contracting muscle, keeping warm.

medium.restatement: The link runs both ways: respiration charges ATP, and splitting it powers the energy-demanding reactions that would otherwise stall.
medium.analogy: A household budget: income from work pays the rent, the food and the heating.
medium.examPointer: Match each ATP use to an example — protein building, a bicep contracting, shivering — for full marks.

check.stem: What does a cell do with ATP to obtain energy?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
ATP turns over constantly; it is not stockpiled.
ATP is made and used inside, never inhaled.
Glucose makes ATP, not the reverse.

check.stem: Which building work is funded by ATP as a cell grows?

options.text: Chemical reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Diffusion needs no ATP payment.
Waste handling is not the cited growth step.
Carbon dioxide is a waste, not a building block.

check.stem: Why does shivering help defend body temperature on a cold day?

options.text: Contraction uses ATP, and the respiration behind it releases heat that warms the body
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Oxygen is used by respiration, not by shaking itself.
No fat is stored during shivering.
It generates heat rather than blocking loss.

check.stem: During muscle contraction, what is the immediate energy source?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Glucose must be respired first; ATP is the immediate payer.
Lactic acid is a waste product, not a payer.
Adrenaline signals; it does not pay.

check.stem: Why is a steady internal temperature useful to an organism?

options.text: Enzymes work best in a narrow range, and warmth from respiration helps maintain it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Extremes denature or slow them.
Waste removal is not the cited reason.
ATP is not the temperature concern; enzymes are.

check.stem: State the full name of the molecule abbreviated ATP.
List three processes funded by ATP.
check.modelAnswer: Building larger molecules, muscle contraction and keeping warm.

check.stem: Explain why respiration and ATP use form a cycle.
check.modelAnswer: Respiration forges ATP from glucose breakdown, and spending ATP on cell work returns it to a lower-energy form that the next round of respiration recharges.

check.stem: A hiker climbs all day then shivers at night. Identify the ATP uses involved.
check.modelAnswer: Contraction powered the climbing, respiration released heat during the effort, and the night-time shivering contracts muscles again to defend body temperature.

glossary.definition: The chemical reaction in all living cells that breaks down glucose and transfers energy into ATP.
Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells break down to fund their work.
The movement of oxygen in and carbon dioxide out — distinct from respiration itself.
